bullets: Inside the building blocks of life: labelling plant and animal cells, meeting the gatekeeper membrane, and climbing from one cell to a whole organism
slides.heading: Cells: structure and organisation
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we label a plant cell and an animal cell, test whether the membrane is a wall or a gatekeeper, meet two specialist structures, find out why plants stand up, and climb the organisation ladder.

bullets: Label the main structures of plant and animal cells and state the job of each one
Explain the membrane as selectively permeable, describe how the vacuole keeps a plant cell firm, and order cells, tissues, organs and systems
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket will ask you to correct the wall idea and to order the organisation ladder.

bullets: A cell stays alive only because things keep moving in and out of it: food and oxygen in, waste out
Yet the cell is wrapped in a membrane - so is that wrapping a solid wall, or something cleverer?
slides.heading: A wall or a gatekeeper?
slides.notes: Ask the class: if the membrane blocked everything, how would the cell eat or breathe? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the membrane turns out to be a gatekeeper, not a wall.

bullets: All living things are made of cells, and each structure inside a cell does one job
Plant cells add three extras an animal cell lacks: a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole
The membrane controls what crosses the border; the nucleus holds the instructions; the cytoplasm is where the work happens
slides.heading: Every structure has a job
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the lesson: structure means function. Every later scene - the gatekeeper, the specialists, the standing-up trick - is one structure doing its one job.

bullets: The labels land one by one: cell wall outside, membrane just inside it, then nucleus, chloroplast and the big vacuole
A plant cell carries the full kit: wall for shape, chloroplasts for making food, vacuole for storage and push
slides.heading: A plant cell, labelled
slides.notes: Narrate each label as it lands and ask the class to point at the same structure on their diagram before you move on.

bullets: The animal cell shows membrane, nucleus and mitochondrion - and no wall, no chloroplast, no big vacuole
With no wall, only the membrane holds the animal cell together, so the membrane job matters even more
slides.heading: An animal cell, labelled
slides.notes: Ask the class to spot what is missing compared with the plant cell; the missing three are exactly the plant extras from the concept slide.

bullets: Food particles cross the membrane into the cell while a blocked particle bounces off: the membrane chooses
A gatekeeper, not a wall: some things pass, others are kept out, and waste is let out
slides.heading: The membrane is the gatekeeper
slides.notes: Watch the crossing closely: one particle enters, one is refused. That choosing is the whole point - the membrane is selectively permeable.

bullets: The nucleus is the control centre: it holds the instructions that run the cell
The chloroplast is the food factory: it traps light energy to make food, and only plant cells have it
slides.heading: Two specialists: nucleus and chloroplast
slides.notes: Give each specialist its one-line job and stress the factory exists only in plant cells, which is why animals must eat.

bullets: Water fills the vacuole until it pushes the membrane hard against the wall: the cell is turgid and firm
Lose the water and the push fades: the cell goes flaccid and the plant wilts
slides.heading: Why plants stand up straight
slides.notes: Act the push with your hands: full vacuole, firm plant; empty vacuole, limp plant. Firmness here is water pressure, not bone.

bullets: Similar cells group into a tissue, tissues build an organ, organs work in a system
The ladder in one line: leaf cell to leaf tissue to leaf to shoot system to the whole plant
slides.heading: Cells team up: the organisation ladder
slides.notes: Climb the ladder one rung at a time with the leaf example, then ask for the animal version: muscle cell, muscle tissue, heart, circulatory system.

bullets: Step 1: a food particle approaches the membrane and crosses into the cell, so the membrane cannot be a solid wall
Step 2: a harmful particle is refused while waste leaves, so the membrane chooses what passes: it is selectively permeable
slides.heading: Worked example: the gatekeeper test
slides.notes: Work this example slowly on the board; it is the exact reasoning the exit ticket asks for.

bullets: An unlabeled animal cell diagram is on your worksheet. Label the membrane, nucleus and mitochondrion, and state one structure it does not have
Careful - a classmate says nothing can enter a cell because the membrane is a solid wall. Explain, using the gatekeeper scene, why the cell would starve if that were true
slides.heading: Your turn: label and explain
slides.notes: Give pairs four minutes; circulate and listen for the wall idea, because the script returns to it at the end.

bullets: On your own: correct the wall claim in one sentence, and write the organisation ladder in order from cell to system
Watch out for the trap one last time: selectively permeable means choosing, not blocking everything
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Collect the tickets at the door; they tell you who still pictures a wall and who owns the gatekeeper idea.
